entries.subject: Chrysochroa fulgidissima
entries.title: Handle with care
entries.body: The giant lifted me on one finger. I gripped it with all six feet. It stopped moving. I stopped moving. Apparently neither of us had done this before.

image.sceneMatch: Bright beetle stands on human fingers; the enormous gentle contact is the scene.

entries.subject: Chrysochroa fulgidissima
entries.title: Summer menu
entries.body: I spent my youth eating the inside of wood. Now I eat leaves in the sunshine. Nobody mentioned there would be a second menu.

entries.subject: Chrysochroa fulgidissima
entries.title: The hole I made
entries.body:
I recognized the old trunk by a bend in the bark. Somewhere inside it was the tunnel I had eaten when I was small.

I had meant to find the opening. Put my head in, perhaps. See whether it still felt enormous.

There were mushrooms all along that side now. Soft orange shelves, one above another. I climbed between them and found a crack just wide enough for my face. The wood crumbled when I touched it.

For a moment I resented them. I had worked very hard on that wood.

Then I remembered what the work had been.

I sat beside the largest mushroom. It had a very fine underside. We said nothing about the trunk.

image.sceneMatch: Beetle climbs an upright old trunk or stump beside large orange fungi. Remembered larval wood feeding, not a pictured larva.

entries.subject: Chrysochroa fulgidissima
entries.title: Depending on the light
entries.body:
A person turned me sideways and said, 'Oh. You're blue.' Turned me back. 'No, green.'

I had been quite certain who was confused until they picked me up.

entries.subject: Chrysoperla carnea group
entries.title: The weather indoors
entries.body:
Rain drove me onto the wall. I found a little dry patch and folded my wings.

A drop slid down beside me. Inside it was a round, upside-down piece of the garden. I went closer. My antenna touched the edge and the entire garden fell apart.

Another drop was coming.

I moved away from that one. Watched the hedge roll down the wall, gather the sky, grow too heavy and go.

When the rain stopped, I stayed for the last few. A perfectly ordinary leaf was waiting outside. I had never been so glad to land on something that kept its shape.

entries.subject: Tettigonia viridissima
entries.title: One foot left
entries.body:
Most of me was out. One back foot was still inside the old one.

I hung there and tried patience. Then force. Then patience again, mainly because force had tired me out.

The empty face above me had its mouth open. It looked astonished. I told it this was hardly helping.

At last the foot slipped free. My new legs were soft. My new wings were crumpled. I held the stem and waited for all of it to become usable.

I'd imagined leaving the old body would feel like making a grand entrance. Mostly I wanted nobody to touch me.

The breeze moved the empty foot. I caught myself worrying that it would lose its grip.

entries.subject: Peripatoides novaezealandiae complex
entries.title: The long dry bit
entries.body:
There was a strip of bare ground between the moss and the log. It had not looked wide until I reached it.

I put my front feet out. The air felt wrong against my skin. I backed up.

A little beetle went across. Didn't even hurry. I disliked him for that, which was unfair.

I waited under the moss until the light thinned. Then longer. A drop touched my back. Another. The smell of the ground changed.

By the time I crossed, the beetle had gone. I had prepared a remark about his hard coat. Quite a good one.

I forgot it halfway. The rain was touching every part of me at once. I took the long way round the twig.

entries.subject: Archispirostreptus gigas
entries.title: The foot that hurt
entries.body:
One foot hurt. I could have carried on without it. There were plenty of others.

But whenever I started walking, I thought of that one little foot, arriving at the ground again.

I stopped. Bent round. There was a bit of grit caught beside it. I worked it loose, then stayed curled while the place stopped aching.

An ant passed and asked what was wrong. I said, 'My foot.'

He looked along me. I knew what he was about to ask. I pointed before he could.

When I started again, I paid attention to that step. It was almost nothing. I went back over the soft patch to feel it once more.

entries.body: He said he liked my eyes. I asked which ones. He panicked and said all of them. I liked that he panicked.

Click here for a larger view as flickr tends to over-sharpen these smaller thumbnails!

Here's yet another image of that beautiful Phidippus regius found during the Florida Bugshot workshop back in August.

This wonderfully fluffy Phidippus regius female (found by a helpful Guillaume Dury) was more than willing to pose for photos from several attendees to the workshop. Given that one of my ultimate goals while in Florida was to find this exact species - I'm grateful that I finally got a chance to photograph one of North America's largest and most beautiful Phidippus species!

The image above is a focus stack of 5(!) shots taken with a 28mm prime reversed on a set of extension tubes. The stacking was done in Zerene Stacker.

In other, non arthropod photography related news, the physics based puzzle platformer video game I've been working on for the past year with Colin and Sarah Northway, Incredipede, has been released! Check out the trailer, complete with all my weird woodcutty illustrations come to life here: www.youtube.com/watch?v=TIxef7gelnI

entries.subject: Phidippus regius
entries.title: When I was little
entries.body:
I saw something enormous bend over my leaf. Two eyes. Only two. Both fixed on me.

I raised my front legs. It moved back.

I had never made anything that large move before. I took a step. It took another step. I was beginning to have an extraordinary opinion of myself.

Then it bent down again and said, very softly, 'Hello.'

The sound went through the leaf and all my feet. I lowered one leg. Left the other up, in case.

We looked at each other for a while. When it went away, I tried the raised leg on a leafhopper.

He left too. But he was leaving already. I try to remember that part.
